roman.title: The Roman Empire
roman.intro: Across the Mediterranean, at the end of Trajan’s reign.
roman.note: Select provinces directly on the map. Boundaries are approximate reconstructions for ca. AD 117 from Harvard’s DARMC, based on the Barrington Atlas. Coastlines and rivers use modern Natural Earth geometry for orientation.

places.name: Roma
places.fact: The imperial capital stood on the Tiber. Trajan’s forum celebrated the emperor whose conquests brought the empire to its widest extent.

places.name: Londinium
places.fact: Roman Londinium grew around a crossing of the Thames, linking river traffic with roads across Britannia.

places.name: Carthago
places.fact: Rebuilt under Roman rule after the destruction of Punic Carthage, this Mediterranean city became a major centre of Roman Africa.

places.name: Alexandria
places.fact: This Mediterranean port connected Egypt’s Nile valley with the wider Roman world. Egypt had been under Roman rule since 30 BC.

places.name: Antiochia
places.fact: Antioch on the Orontes was a leading city in Roman Syria, near routes linking the Mediterranean with inland Asia.

places.name: Ephesus
places.fact: A major city of the Roman province of Asia, Ephesus lay near the Aegean coast in western Anatolia.

places.name: Britannia
places.modern: Much of present-day England and Wales
places.fact: The Roman province occupied part of Britain. The island’s northern regions remained beyond direct Roman provincial rule.

places.name: Hispania Baetica
places.fact: Baetica occupied the south of the Iberian Peninsula. This marker represents the province rather than a city.

places.name: Gallia Lugdunensis
places.fact: One of the provinces of Roman Gaul, named for Lugdunum, modern Lyon. Its geography does not match a modern national border.

places.name: Aegyptus
places.fact: Rome governed Egypt as a province. The Nile valley was central to its agriculture and connections with the Mediterranean.

places.name: Dacia
places.fact: Trajan’s Dacian conquests added territory north of the Danube to Roman rule in the early second century.

places.name: Africa Proconsularis
places.modern: Mainly present-day Tunisia and adjacent areas
places.fact: This Roman province faced Italy across the central Mediterranean. Its provincial name did not mean the entire continent of Africa.

medieval.title: The Middle Ages
medieval.intro: Kingdoms, empires and cities of the high medieval world.
medieval.scope: Europe, North Africa and the eastern Mediterranean
medieval.note: Select mapped realms directly. Boundaries are approximate reconstructions around AD 1200 from Harvard’s DARMC. Some later polities in the source layer are omitted. Coastlines and rivers provide modern geographic orientation; medieval sovereignty was often overlapping or disputed.

places.name: Kingdom of England
places.fact: Around 1200, England was ruled by the Plantagenet dynasty. King John’s reign began in 1199; Magna Carta followed in 1215.

places.name: Kingdom of Scotland
places.fact: Scotland was a separate kingdom in this period. Its medieval political history should not be read through the later United Kingdom.

places.name: Kingdom of France
places.fact: Royal authority and the power of regional lords overlapped in medieval France. A single location marker cannot represent all its changing frontiers.

places.name: Holy Roman Empire
places.fact: A complex empire of principalities and other territories in central Europe. It was distinct from the ancient Roman Empire.

places.name: Byzantine Empire
places.fact: In AD 1200 Constantinople was still the Byzantine imperial capital. The Fourth Crusade captured it in 1204, after this expedition’s reference date.

places.name: Almohad Caliphate
places.modern: North Africa and part of Iberia
places.fact: The Almohads ruled across parts of North Africa and southern Iberia around 1200. Their architecture connected both shores of the western Mediterranean.

places.name: London
places.fact: London stood within the Plantagenet kingdom of England, whose rulers also held lands across the English Channel.

places.name: Paris
places.fact: Paris was an important royal and intellectual centre in medieval France. The period saw growing royal authority and urban life.

places.name: Venice
places.fact: Venice was a maritime republic linked to Mediterranean trade. Its ships would play a central role in the Fourth Crusade after 1200.

places.name: Constantinople
places.fact: The city on the Bosporus linked Europe and Asia. Its medieval inhabitants considered themselves Romans; “Byzantine” is a later historical label.

places.name: Toledo
places.fact: Toledo was a major city of Christian-ruled Iberia by 1200, within a peninsula of several kingdoms and Islamic states.

places.name: Palermo
places.fact: Palermo was an important centre of the Kingdom of Sicily, where Latin, Greek and Arabic cultural traditions had interacted.
